name: Maya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work days at a big online fashion warehouse, the kind that ships dresses and trainers next-day. I'm on a pick-to-light station, so lights on the shelves tell me which slot to grab from and the screen tells me which bag it goes in. In the afternoon I usually move to returns, checking that people didn't send back a dress with fake tan on it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the speed and the people, and I'm one of the ones they ask when the scanners play up. What wears me down is the repetition, the same reach a thousand times before lunch. On the side I sell vintage jackets online, and I use an AI tool every day to write the listings and price them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I already use AI for my listings and it saves me maybe an hour a week, so that's roughly what this sounds like. The warehouse would just keep humming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a handy helper, not a job killer, and that people should stop being scared of it. At work I'd show a couple of the girls how I write my listings with it, because they always ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a little disappointing. I'm the person who likes new kit. A world where nothing changes means I keep doing the same reach a thousand times. But money-wise I'm safe, with ten months saved and some shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, keep growing the vintage shop, and maybe aim for team leader within two years. I'd put another 300 a month into my index fund, which is a cheap fund that follows the whole stock market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit restless. Like being on a train that's on time but slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would becoming a team leader mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 2,000 a year more, and fewer reaches. My shift manager Dev already lets me cover breaks on the returns line. It's not a dream, but it's a step up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the vintage shop right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small, maybe 250 a month after costs. I buy jackets at car boot sales on Sundays and list them that night. It's more fun than money, but it's growing.

say: AI is a **handy helper**, not a job killer, so people should relax.
I'd show colleagues how I write **listings** with AI, since they keep asking.
think: Money-wise I'm **safe**, with ten months saved and some shares.
Part of me finds a world where nothing changes **disappointing** and slow.
do: Put another **300 a month** into an index fund.
Grow the **vintage jacket** shop beyond 250 a month.
Aim for **team leader** on the returns line within two years.
feel: Calm but **restless**, like a train that's on time but slow.
S0.quote: I'm the person who likes new kit. A world where nothing changes means I keep doing the same reach a thousand times.
fieldNote: She is the rare worker **disappointed** by the calm scenario.
Her AI use comes from a **side business**, not from the warehouse.
Savings and shares give her a **secure base** for small bets.

steps.text: Keep working days on the pick-to-light station
Add 300 a month to her index fund
List more vintage jackets from Sunday car boot sales

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more interesting. The thinking tasks going first means the office and the customer service team at head office. On the floor, robots creep in slowly, which our site has already started with those shelf-carrying robots in the new wing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for floor staff, not just a threat. Somebody has to run the robot wing, clear jams and train new starters. I'd say it loudly at work, because I want that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the pickers who don't move will get squeezed, and I don't intend to be one of them. My picking hours would shrink, but I'd be first in line for the robot wing. With my savings I can afford a pay dip while I switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dev this month to put me forward as a super-user for the robot wing, which is the person who knows the system best on each shift. I'd do the vendor's online training course on my own time. I'd also use AI to put my shop's pricing on autopilot so I have more evenings free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe even excited. I know that sounds strange for a picker, but this one looks good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, mostly, who won't touch a touchscreen. Tomasz is 54 and picks faster than anyone. Being the fastest won't matter when the shelves come to you. I'd try to get him on the training with me, but I know he'd say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it looks good for you. What would make you wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company brings in its own engineers from outside and leaves us on the old wing until it shuts. That happens. I'd give it a year, and if I'm not in, I'd apply to the newer sites on the motorway that are fully robotic.

say: This is a **chance** for floor staff to run the robots, not just a threat.
Somebody has to **clear jams** and train new starters, and I want that job.
think: Pickers who don't move will get **squeezed**, and I won't be one of them.
My savings let me **afford a pay dip** while I switch roles.
do: Ask Dev **this month** to make her robot-wing super-user.
Take the robot vendor's **online training** in her own time.
Use AI to put the shop's **pricing on autopilot**.
feel: Calm and even **excited**, because this picture looks good for her.
S1.quote: Tomasz is 54 and picks faster than anyone. Being the fastest won't matter when the shelves come to you.
fieldNote: She reads the robot wing as a **promotion path**, not a threat.
Her one worry is the company bringing in **outside engineers**.
Her concern for older colleague **Tomasz** is real, but she'd still move on.

steps.text: Ask her shift manager to make her the robot-wing super-user
Complete the robot vendor's online training course
Set AI to price the vintage shop automatically
Apply to fully robotic sites on the motorway if passed over

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one stops me. The thinking AI by 2028 and robots that can pick like people by 2031. The robot wing job I wanted is a thinking job, mostly. AGI could take it before the robots even take the picking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say we need rules, like companies sharing the savings with the workers they replace. I'd post about it, which I never do, because this would affect everyone in my building at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my plan from the slow picture falls apart. Supervising robots is screens and decisions, and that's exactly what AGI does by 2028. Then by 2031 the picking is gone too, so I'd lose the job at both ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd pull my savings into cash, so I'm not caught by a crash in shares. I'd grow the vintage shop hard, because people buying old jackets from a real person feels like something AI can't fake. I'd look at hands-on trades with a human side, like hairdressing or fitting kitchens, and start one before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really. I'm still the one who moves first, but I don't know which direction is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my runway, basically. The warehouse would still pay me until about 2031, so I'd use those three years to build something on the side. If I'm still only a picker in 2031, I've wasted the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell shares in a world where AI makes companies richer. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, maybe. My head says the big firms win, so shares should go up. My gut says a crash comes first, and I'd rather keep my rent money safe than be clever. I'd keep a little in.

say: We need **rules** so companies share their savings with the workers they replace.
I'd **post publicly** about it, which I never usually do.
think: Supervising robots is screen work, so AGI takes that **target job** by 2028.
By 2031 the picking goes too, so I'd lose the job **at both ends**.
do: Move most of her **shares into cash** in the first year, keeping a little invested.
Grow the **vintage shop** hard as a human business AI can't fake.
Choose and start a **hands-on trade** like hairdressing or kitchen fitting before 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, still ready to move first but unsure which way is safe.
S2.quote: The robot wing job I wanted is a thinking job, mostly. AGI could take it before the robots even take the picking.
fieldNote: The fast picture **breaks her plan**: her target job is thinking work.
She treats the three years as a **runway** to build something else.
She admits a **contradiction** about shares and keeps a little in.

steps.text: Grow the vintage jacket shop into a real second income
Start a hands-on trade course such as hairdressing before 2031
Move most of her shares into cash savings
Post online calling for firms to share automation savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, so AGI by 2031 and robots by 2034. Like with the fast one, the supervisor job is the weak spot. But five years is enough to try two or three things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where workers should be planning now and companies should be helping. I'd say it at the canteen table and I'd share the training courses I find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well here. I'd still take the robot wing job for a couple of years, because it pays more and looks good on a CV. Then I'd step off before 2031 into something that's people plus hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, robot wing super-user plus the vendor course. I'd grow the shop to maybe 600 a month and test whether it could be full-time. I'd keep the index fund going, because five years is long enough to ride out a dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a fizzy way. It's on my mind every day, but I feel like I'm holding the steering wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you live, if the shop went full-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not here. Rent by the warehouse park is cheap, but the vintage buyers are in the city. I'd think about moving closer to the markets in year three or four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self starting at the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every scanner I learned at 22 is already in a skip. Learn every system, but don't marry any of them. I'd tell myself to save, which I did, thank God.

say: Workers should be **planning now**, and companies should be helping them.
I'd **share training courses** I find with people at the canteen table.
think: I'd take the **robot wing job** for a few years because it pays more.
Then I'd **step off before 2031** into work that's people plus hands.
do: Become robot-wing **super-user** and finish the vendor course in year one.
Grow the shop to about **600 a month** to test going full-time.
Keep paying into the **index fund** through any dip.
feel: Uneasy in a **fizzy** way, but holding the steering wheel.
S3.quote: Every scanner I learned at 22 is already in a skip. Learn every system, but don't marry any of them.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **use the robot job** as a stepping stone.
She'd consider **moving** to the city for the vintage trade.
Her motto is to learn systems but **not marry** them.

steps.text: Take the robot-wing super-user role and vendor course
Grow the vintage shop to about 600 a month
Keep paying 300 a month into the index fund
Plan a move nearer the city vintage markets by year four

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, AGI by 2036 and robots by 2039. I'd be nearly 40. That's basically a whole second career with time to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone my age to be caught out, and that employers and the government should fund proper retraining. I'd be the annoying one sending course links to the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the warehouse is a chapter for me, not the book. I'd ride the robot wing for a few years, build the shop, and by my mid-thirties be doing something where people come to me because they trust me. The robots arriving in 2039 would just be the last push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing dramatic: robot wing role, vendor course, 300 a month into the fund. I'd start a weekend course in clothing repair and alterations, because fixing a jacket by hand fits my shop. Maybe I'd go part-time at the warehouse in year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy, because it's still the same end point. But I'd have so much room that it feels more like a project than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the same end point to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A world where machines do both the thinking and the lifting. Ten years doesn't change that, it just changes whether I meet it with a plan. And I don't know what's left after that, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, actually. My mum ran a tailoring shop for 15 years. She'd teach me alterations for free if I bought her lunch, so my retraining budget is sorted.

say: Nobody my age has an **excuse** to be caught out with ten years' warning.
Employers and government should fund **proper retraining** for warehouse staff.
think: The warehouse is **a chapter**, not the whole book, for me.
By my mid-thirties I'd want work where people come for **trust**.
do: Keep the robot-wing role and put **300 a month** into the fund.
Start a weekend course in **clothing alterations** with her mum's help.
Go **part-time** at the warehouse around year three.
feel: Mostly **uneasy**, but it feels more like a **project** than a threat.
S4.quote: My mum ran a tailoring shop for 15 years. She'd teach me alterations for free if I bought her lunch, so my retraining budget is sorted.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her shift into **a project**, not a rescue.
She still names the **same end point** and doesn't know what's left after it.
Her mum's old **tailoring shop** gives her a real skills path.

steps.text: Learn clothing alterations from her mum, who ran a tailoring shop
Add repairs to the vintage jacket shop
Keep paying 300 a month into the index fund
Drop to part-time at the warehouse around year three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My whole plan was to climb into the robot wing, and that one takes the ladder away at the top and the bottom. What would help is cheap, fast courses for hands-on people trades, paid while you still have a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I like my job. I like the warehouse fine, but I don't love it, and that makes change easier. People who love the warehouse are the ones I'd worry about.

headlineQuote: I like the warehouse fine, but I don't love it, and that makes change easier. People who love the warehouse are the ones I'd worry about.
portrait: Maya is a 27-year-old **pick-to-light** worker at an online fashion warehouse.
She runs a small **vintage jacket** shop and uses AI daily for listings.
In the slow pictures she sees the **robot wing** as her promotion path.
AGI by 2028 breaks that plan, since supervising robots is **thinking work**.
With more warning she'd learn **alterations** from her mum and build a people-and-hands business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it removes her **ladder** at both the top and the bottom.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast **courses in hands-on trades**, paid while people still have a job.
